file: 1_1_00_ AROUND THE WORLD_Ancient Temple in Tokyo Rings In Just a New Year.txt
text:
ï»¿
As the monks in their long black robes and golden sashes put the finishing touches on preparations for the New Year celebrations here, there was little room for doubt that this was a big day for Zojoji Temple, one of Tokyo's great Buddhist houses of worship.
There was the altar to be prepared in front of the huge bronze bell to be sounded 108 times to relieve the soul of its many agonies and frustrations.
There was the huge tarpaulin-like collection vessel to be strung up and secured to gather in the many pounds of coins to be tossed in offering. 
And there were the helium balloons to be filled that at the right moment would carry people's prayers skyward.
But as that moment drew near, conversations with the people who filled the sprawling grounds of the huge complex to the bursting point made clear that for Japanese, from the Buddhist cleric to the high school lovebirds strolling arm in arm, the celebration of the New Year, always a huge event for the nation's Buddhist temples and Shinto shrines, was only incidentally related to the global hoopla about the year 2000.
Almost every aspect of the millennium events here bore reminders that Japan, more than any other place on earth, has managed to absorb all of the outward trappings of the Western world while at the same time remaining profoundly, and quite proudly, different.
Indeed, the Tokyo television tower, a replica of the Eiffel Tower that glowed brightly close by at the stroke of midnight, seemed like a neon advertisement of the dichotomy, as visitors crowding the temple grounds snatched up the last of the white arrows on sale there to be hung in the home to ward off evil, while clerics blew the reedy, ancient court music, or gagaku, from their flutes.
And then there was the sermon delivered by Kyoshin Todo, the elaborately robed head monk of this temple, which was founded in 880.
"It has been 1999 years since the birth of Christ, but Buddha was living long before then," he said, stooping deeply as he clutched a long white hairy whisk. 
"We have all -- whether Japanese or Chinese or Indian Buddhists -- gone over to keeping dates this way. 
If the Buddha were alive today, what would he think?
"He wouldn't say anything, because he has a huge heart. 
And that is what God is trying to teach us, that we must accept each other."
In fact, Japanese have a wide variety of choices for keeping calendars, from the birth of Buddha, in 563 B.C., to the imperial-based date system still in official use. 
This year is Heisei 12, the 12th year of Emperor Akihito's reign, according to that method.
There are others, too, from the traditional Chinese lunar calendar to the Shinto dating system, whose count begins with the reign of Jimmu, the mythical, divinely born first emperor, starting in 660 B.C. The celebration of the new year on Jan. 
1 only began with the introduction of the Gregorian calendar and other Western inventions under the Meiji Restoration of 1868.
Still, the little lecture, which seemed in part a mild reproach to Asians for having forsaken many of their traditions for Western ways, seemed almost redundant, judging from the comments of those who flocked here. 
Almost none of them said they regarded the start of the new year as an entry into a new era in the first place.
"Mill, millen, millennium," Yaeko Mizoguchi, a 60-year-old woman said, laughing as she struggled with the word borrowed from English. 
"We are Japanese. 
It is too hard to pronounce, and we cannot be bothered with it anyway."
Her husband, Mutsumi Mizoguchi, 63, a retired engineer, added: "We have our own culture to live in, just as Americans have theirs. 
We enjoy our own traditions, our own flags, our own songs. 
When you celebrate your own culture properly, then you can go forth into the world proudly."
The couple said they had been celebrating the New Year in the same way all their lives. 
But young couples who turned out here in large numbers showed no greater interest in the millennium and no less fidelity to this country's traditions.
Buddhism came to Japan from China and Korea in the sixth century and gradually took its place alongside Shinto, the ancient indigenous animistic religion, as one of the country's two principal forms of worship. 
Although it has not always been the case, the two now live in a sort of easy cohabitation.
Japanese pick and choose which of the two religions to use to mark important moments during the year, often on the basis of nothing more spiritual than which temple or shrine is closest to their homes.
"To be honest, we don't have much faith," said Yukio Hoshi, 28, a salaryman who came to the temple to make New Year's wishes with his girlfriend, Akiko Kuji. 
"More than anything else, we've come here out of habit. 
This is how you celebrate occasions like this in Japan."
At a long table provided for the occasion, the couple carefully filled out cards listing their wishes for the new year and then joined the long line to enter the temple where a golden Buddha sat atop a richly decorated altar. 
Their wishes?
"Health for our families, success in work and happiness together," said Miss Kuji, 25, tugging a blanket around her shoulders against the cold.
For most young couples, Christmas is the biggest time for year-end parties. 
New Year's, by contrast, is traditionally a quiet, contemplative holiday, when ancestors are remembered, people seek atonement and make new wishes, and families draw close.
"At this time of year I believe Japanese are seeking renewal and spiritual refreshment," said Nichihiro Kuya, a monk who is director of publications for Zojoji Temple. 
"That's pretty much the same thing that Westerners are seeking too, isn't it?"
Asked how he felt about the ease with which Japanese people switch among religions, including Christianity, which claims less than 1 percent of the population as regular worshipers but whose wedding rites are wildly popular here, he managed to find a virtue. 
"Japanese have a history of flexibility, and will accept anything if they think it is good, whether it is Buddhist, Shinto or a Christian-style wedding," he said. 
"Of course we would like as many believers as possible for our sect, but this adaptability is a strong point of our culture."

file: ATLANTA_ DAY 11 -- SOFTBALL_One More Victory to Nail U.S. Gold.txt
text:
ï»¿
The United States is one victory away from winning a gold medal in softball.
But what a battle to get there. 
It took a typical pitching performance by Lisa Fernandez (a three-hitter and 13 strikeouts) and a 10th-inning bases-loaded single by Sheila Cornell tonight to beat a stubborn Chinese team, 1-0.
The victory sent the United States into the championship game Tuesday night against Australia or China. 
Australia beat Japan, 2-0, in tonight's second game, on home runs by Kerry Dienelt and Haylee Petrie and Tanya Harding's two-hit pitching. 
Australia will play China at 4:30 P.M. Tuesday, and that winner moves on to the 7 P.M. final against the United States.
International softball officials created the peculiar setup to reward the team with the best record in the round-robin preliminary round, in this case the United States (6-1).
After the game, the Americans were drained, and not just from the 87-degree temperature and 51 percent humidity.
"When you miss so many opportunities," said Dot Richardson, the American shortstop, "it drains you. 
This has been a very emotional tournament for us because of so many close games."
The doubleheader at downtown Golden Park drew a sellout crowd of 8,729, including Juan Antonio Samaranch, the president of the International Olympic Committee. 
Scalpers were asking $200 for $32 tickets.
Fernandez is a 25-year-old California-bred right-hander with a fastball that reaches 66 miles an hour, a huge problem for batters only 40 feet away.
For six innings, she pitched a perfect game, and the Chinese could not even hit the ball out of the infield.
The perfect game ended when Zhang Chunfang led off the Chinese seventh with a single. 
The only hits Fernandez allowed were chipped singles that fell in front of outfielders.
But for nine innings, her teammates could not get a run. 
In the third, Julie Smith, trying to score from second base on a single to right field, was thrown out. 
In the sixth, with two Americans on base, Zhang, the Chinese center fielder, misjudged Danielle Tyler's long fly before grabbing it just in front of the fence.
Softball games usually last seven innings. 
If the game is tied after seven, the eighth and (if necessary) ninth innings are played under normal rules.
If the score is still tied after nine, international rules dictate that each half-inning start with a runner on second base.
In the 10th, Richardson was that gift runner. 
Julie Smith, the leadoff batter, was hit in the right thigh by a pitch, putting Americans on first and second. 
Then Dionna Harris grounded to shortstop. 
The throw to third base to force Richardson hit her in the back, and the bases were loaded.
"I purposely didn't slide," Richardson said, "because I was trying to get hit. 
Luckily for me, it worked. 
I've never been so happy to get hit by a ball."
So now the bases were loaded with none out. 
China's relief pitcher, Wang Lihong, struck out the next batter, Kim Maher.
Up came Cornell, a 5-foot-8-inch, 178-pound first baseman and, like Richardson, a 34-year-old veteran of the Americans' 10-year climb to the top.
"When I stepped to the plate," Cornell said, "I said to myself, 'This is where I want to be.'
I love being able to make or break the game. 
I wasn't trying to hit a home run because we just needed one run."
Cornell ran the count to 3-0, then took a called strike. 
On the next pitch, she hit a sharp grounder between second base and the diving Chinese second baseman, Yan Fang. 
Before Cornell left the batter's box, she was grinning and pumping her arms because she knew the ball would get through the infield. 
It did, Richardson scored and the Americans won.
For Fernandez, the victory was revenge of sorts. 
Because she has a tender ankle, this was only her second appearance in these Olympics. 
The first was last Friday, when she struck out 15, retired 29 straight batters and pitched a perfect game against Australia until there were two out in the 10th. 
Then, with the United States leading by 1-0 and an 0-2 count against Joanne Brown, a rising pitch by Fernandez hung over the center of the plate, Brown knocked it over the fence and Australia won, 2-1, the only American loss here.
"In the top of the 10th tonight," Fernandez said, "China had a runner on second and I kept saying, 'Not again, not again, not again.'
I reached for something extra. 
I found my energy from my teammates."

file: ATLANTA_ DAY 14 -- SOCCER_Women_s Soccer_ 76,481 Fans, 1 U.S. Gold.txt
text:
ï»¿
They have been together a long time close to a decade for some of them -- and tonight the American women won a prize they could not have imagined when they began assembling. 
By beating a spirited and talented China, 2-1, they won a gold medal in the first women's soccer tournament in Summer Games history.
Tiffeny Milbrett scored the historic goal in the 68th minute at the end of a fast break begun by Mia Hamm on the right side, who pushed the ball to Joy Fawcett in the middle, who set up Milbrett racing in from the left.
The attendance was 76,481, apparently the largest crowd to watch a women's game anywhere in the world. 
Last Sunday's crowd of 64,196 was the largest to see the women's team in this country, just shy of the 65,000 that saw them play the World Cup final in Guangzhou, China, in 1991. 
Team officials said there is no record of any women's team -- in any sport, in any country -- playing before a larger crowd.
However, almost nothing of the game was shown on NBC, and afterward, Hank Steinbrecher, the executive director of the United States Soccer Federation, blasted the network, saying, "NBC must think the world is full of divers."
In renovated Sanford Stadium at the University of Georgia, where the fabled hedges were cut back to allow for more seating, the public-address announcer called the sport "football," the way most of the world does.
This jittery championship, after the United States had been outhustled during the middle of the match, is the second world victory for the United States. 
The women won the first women's World Cup in 1991 in China, finished third in the second World Cup in Sweden in 1995 and paved the way for the 1999 World Cup to be held in the United States.
And they had played together long enough to be a real team, like the New York Islanders used to be, like the old Boston Celtics.
You could read it in the "caps," the soccer term for international appearances: Kristine Lilly with 121, the sore-legged Hamm with 120, Carin Gabarra, who replaced Hamm in the closing minutes, earned her 117th, and Michelle Akers would have had more than 109 caps but for her struggle with the debilitating Epstein-Barr virus in recent years.
Fawcett made her 101st appearance tonight. 
Fawcett celebrated the victory by holding her 2-year-old daughter, Katelyn Rose, in her arms as she waved to the fans after the semifinal victory over Norway.
Tonight, Carla Overbeck, the star defender, played her 100th game and received the traditional engraved watch, Julie Foudy reached 96 caps, Tisha Venturini 71, Milbrett 65, Tiffany Roberts came on late for Milbrett and played in her 54th, goalkeeper Briana Scurry reached 46 and Brandi Chastain toughed it out with her right leg heavily taped and reached 40.
And Shannon MacMillan, in the starting lineup tonight, reached 28 caps and scored the first goal in the 18th minute, a goal involving 378 games of international experience. 
The weary but wise Akers trapped a loose ball at midfield and sent it wide to the left for Lilly, who dribbled downfield and turned the corner, firing the ball left-footed. 
It ricocheted out to Hamm, who shot on goal, and the rebound went to MacMillan, who put the ball into the net.
Then the Americans went into a shell, apparently trying to contain the Chinese rather than attack. 
Akers was hobbling, apparently with leg cramps, and the Americans seemed listless. 
They paid for it in the 32d minute when Sun Wen got past Overbeck and chipped the ball over Scurry, who had left the goalmouth.
Some aggressive work by Hamm woke the United States from its lethargy. 
Women's soccer does not have the booming power or the intricate negative defenses of world-level men's soccer. 
The way to go in women's soccer is full speed ahead.
Hamm chases the ball obsessively, the way Pete Rose used to pursue base hits. 
She tore up her ankle in the second game of this tournament. 
Coach Tony DiCicco has been complaining about the rules allowing only 16 players a team for a five-game schedule in 12 days. 
The women had just enough left to produce the burst of energy for the gold medal.
China did not lack for support, with three separate clusters of yellow-and-red-clad fans waving bright red banners and flags and dancing to the halftime tunes like "Y.M.C.A." by the Village People.
Norway, which lost a heartbreaking semifinal to the United States on Sunday, won the bronze medal tonight with a 2-0 victory over Brazil. 
Linda Medalen deliberately set up a goal in front by Ann Aarones in the 21st minute and Aarones boomed an untouchable rocket in the 25th minute.
Soccer or football, it is now an Olympic sport for women, and it fills stadiums. 
And the first champion is a team that stuck together for a decade for this night, when the players would run around an American football field in front of 76,481 fans.

file: ATLANTA_ DAY 15 -- DIVING_For First Time in 84 Years, Americans Miss Out on Gold.txt
text:
ï»¿
Greg Louganis stopped by the Georgia Tech Aquatic Center earlier this week. 
He was working as a television reporter, and his presence was a nagging reminder of how much American divers have slipped since he wrung out his chamois for the last time after winning two more gold medals at the 1988 Summer Olympics.
The Americans ended up winning no golds in Atlanta, and the last time that happened in an Olympics in which Americans competed was 1912 in Stockholm.
They could not manage a medal of any color in tonight's final event: the men's 10-meter platform, in which Dmitri Sautin of Russia put an end to China's hopes of an Olympic sweep.
Sautin, the reigning world champion, did it with a superb, steady performance, receiving no score lower than a 7.5 on any of his six dives and consistently receiving scores of 9.0 or higher.
On his final effort -- a back one-and-a-half somersault with three-and-a-half twists -- he received the only perfect 10 awarded during the men's competition (the other six judges settled for 9.0's and 9.5's).
"I was very mad at myself," said Sautin of his surprisingly low fifth-place finish in the men's springboard competition. 
"So I came out and managed to accomplish what I needed to accomplish on platform."
Sautin, the first Russian or Soviet to win the Olympic platform title, finished sixth in this event in 1992. 
That was less than a year after he was stabbed in the stomach several times during a fight. 
He nearly died from loss of blood and spent two months in a Russian hospital. 
Since then, he has reasserted his imposing, if not always graceful, presence.
"Sautin's not a style diver," said American Coach Ron O'Brien. 
"He's a power, acrobatic, good-entry diver."
He took the lead from Jan Hempel of Germany after the first round in tonight's final and never relinquished it, scoring no lower than 76.50 on any of his six dives and winning by a comfortable 29.07 points. 
Hempel settled for the silver; Xiao Hailiang of China for the bronze, which means that China won 5 of the 12 diving medals awarded in Atlanta.
David Pichler of the United States was sixth; Patrick Jeffrey was ninth, which means that the United States won only two medals in Atlanta: a bronze from Mary Ellen Clark on women's platform and another bronze from Mark Lenzi on men's springboard.
That is hardly a major surprise. 
The Americans won no golds in the 1994 world championships in Rome. 
Nor did they win any in the four Olympic events contested at the 1995 Pan American Games.
The trend continued here despite the support of a large and unabashedly partisan crowd. 
The Americans were far from abysmal. 
All eight United States divers qualified for the finals, something no other delegation accomplished, not even the Chinese. 
But they could not rise (or better yet, fall) to the highest level.
"We need to take another look at our program," O'Brien said. 
"We have done it to some degree, but we were late reacting. 
It's not that our guys have gotten worse. 
It's just that others have made great improvements."
Today's finals were a case in point. 
Neither Pichler nor Jeffrey made a major error, and yet when the last dive had been completed, they were well off the pace. 
At 31, Jeffrey is the oldest male diver in Atlanta. 
He competed in the 1988 Olympics, where he contracted a virus and finished 12th.
"I'm a little disappointed, but I'm not upset," he said. 
"I'm walking out with my head up."
While Jeffrey was waxing sanguine, his competitors were dividing the spoils. 
The Chinese had won the first three events in Atlanta, with Fu Mingxia winning on both the women's platform and springboard and Xiong Ni winning on the men's springboard. 
But Xiao and the 16-year-old Tian Liang -- both competing in their first Olympics -- would be unable to complete the first Olympic sweep in 44 years.
"We were new divers; this was our first time in a competition like this," said the 19-year-old Xiao. 
"We wanted to win the fourth gold for our country, but we were not under any pressure to win it."
Sautin was simply too good, his scores too consistently high. 
They were the kinds of scores that once were the rule for a man named Louganis. 
But Louganis is now reporting for television, and the Americans are no longer dominant.

file: Chinese Lose Swim Medals.txt
text:
ï»¿
Eleven Chinese competitors from the Asian Games in Hiroshima, Japan, in October were stripped of their medals yesterday after testing positive for drugs, the Olympic Council of Asia said.
A council statement said urine samples of the 11 competitors all showed traces of Dehydrotestosterone, or DHT, a drug banned by the International Olympic Committee.
Two of those named, Lu Bin of the women's team and Xiong Guoming of the men's team, each won four gold medals in swimming at the games.

file: Chinese Swimming Bans Champion.txt
text:
ï»¿
Following the lead of the international swimming federation, FINA, the Chinese Swimming Association banned the world champion Yang Aihua today after she failed a drug test.
The Chinese organization issued a statement confirming FINA's announcement Wednesday that Yang had been banned after testing positive for an excessive level of testosterone. 
A random test was taken Sept. 
30 before the Asian Games at Hiroshima, Japan.
Yang won the 400-meter freestyle silver medal at the games in Hiroshima and the gold medal in the same event at the world championships in Rome in September. 
She tested negative in Rome, the official Xinhua News Agency reported. 
The suspension will last through Sept. 
29, 1996, keeping Yang out of the 1996 Atlanta Olympics.
Chinese officials repeatedly have denied allegations of systematic drug use by their women swimmers, who won 12 of 16 titles at Rome and set 5 world records.

file: GOODWILL GAMES_Wilkinson Leading the U.S. Toward a Diving Comeback.txt
text:
ï»¿
Until the 1980's, the world's best divers usually came from the United States and its college and club systems. 
Then the Chinese discovered and developed the sport, the Russians made a resurgence, the great American champion Greg Louganis retired and American diving struggled.
Now the Americans seem to be making a small comeback, although when the Goodwill Games diving competition ended tonight, China and Russia had won the most medals. 
After 9 of the 10 events, China had 12 medals (4 gold), Russia 7 (4 gold), the United States 3 (1 gold) and the rest of the world 5. 
The best diver here was Dmitri Sautin, a Russian who won the men's 3-meter springboard on Sunday and the 10-meter platform tonight.
But the Americans made a strong impression Sunday night when 20-year-old Laura Wilkinson, a University of Texas junior from Houston, won the women's platform title. 
Wilkinson had won seven United States championships, but never a big international competition. 
And this one was big. 
The field included the world champion (Olena Zhupina of Ukraine) and runner-up (Cai Yuyan of China).
Here, every contender except Wilkinson made at least one major error -- an overrotation here, an underrotation there, a failure to keep the knees straight or the legs together. 
Wilkinson made no big mistakes. 
And when she needed a solid last dive to overtake Cai, she made it, a back 1 1/2 somersault with 2 1/2 twists, that drew scores of 8.0 from all seven judges.
Starting the ninth and last round, Wilkinson trailed Cai. 
Then Cai, only 16 but more experienced than Wilkinson, barely finished a 3 1/2 somersault pike. 
The door was open for Wilkinson, who dived next. 
She said her nervousness disappeared, and she nailed her dive. 
But she said that for her and for the American team, this was only one competition.
"I need to keep working on everything," she said. 
"And since the other teams are so good, we've had to work twice as hard to be able to compete with them. 
I think we're making progress. 
I don't know if it was U.S. diving slipping so much as the Chinese and Russians getting better."
Li Hongping of Mission Viejo, Calif., a former Chinese champion and one of the three coaches of this American team, was cheered by Wilkinson's victory.
"It's very significant," he said, "because it shows our divers are as competent as anyone else. 
This builds confidence in her and in the whole diving program in the U.S.
"It's very difficult to compete with someone who is training more, like the Chinese and the Russians. 
We have to be mentally tougher than anyone and have a more positive attitude. 
I'm seeing that. 
It happened with Laura and that's why she won a gold medal, so this is a very good step."

file: I.O.C. Pressured to Make Beijing a Forbidden City.txt
text:
ï»¿
Human Rights Watch, an organization that monitors human rights abuses worldwide, is lobbying International Olympic Committee members in an attempt to gain I.O.C. opposition to Beijing's bid to hold the 2000 Summer Olympic Games.
Robert Bernstein, chairman of Human Rights Watch, said his United States-based organization received "an unacceptable response" from the I.O.C. after his group had sent a letter to the I.O.C.'s president, Juan Antonio Samaranch, protesting the consideration of China as a host country.
Bernstein said that Human Rights Watch might ask athletes to boycott the 2000 Olympics if China were selected as the site.
"The Olympics would be an enormous plum for the Chinese Government," Bernstein said. 
"China would put people away and clean up the city like you wouldn't believe. 
It would be great for the economy. 
The Government would be able to say it was well respected by the world community, while it was still torturing prisoners."
The 93-member I.O.C. will select the site for the 2000 Olympics at its September meeting in Monte Carlo, Monaco. 
The members have begun to travel to potential Olympic sites, which include Sydney, Australia; Manchester, England; Brasilia, Istanbul, Turkey; and Berlin. 
Sydney is considered the favorite, but Beijing has support among I.O.C. members who wish to open the Games to another part of the world.
Anita DeFrantz, the only I.O.C. member from the United States, said she intended to visit Beijing, as well as all the other bidding cities, before making a decision.
"I know the arguments that the opponents of the Beijing bid are making," she said. 
"I am also aware that the United States tends to be on top of many lists for human-rights violations."
Recently, China has released several priests and other political prisoners. 
Skeptical observers believe this is part of a public relations campaign to land the Olympics. 
In addition, I.O.C. members have been assured by local and regional officials in China that there will be no opposition expressed to their visits.
A report by Asia Watch, one of the groups under the umbrella of Human Rights Watch, stated that the campaign of Deng Xiaoping for economic reform "had not prevented new arrests, arbitrary detention, prejudged political trials, torture, and other human rights abuses in 1992."
In response to his complaint to the I.O.C., Bernstein received a letter from Jean-Mishal Gunz, a deputy director of the I.O.C., that stated, "Your comments are duly noted, and we appreciate you keeping us informed."
Bernstein said that this response was inadequate and that his organization would begin an organized campaign aimed at all 93 I.O.C. voting members.
Human Rights Watch has also charged Turkey and Brazil, other Olympic bidders, with serious rights abuses. 
But Bernstein said that China was by far the worst offender.
"The others simply are not as bad," Bernstein said.

file: In Beijing Students_ Worldview, Jordan Rules.txt
text:
ï»¿
It was class time at Beijing University, but at 10 this morning seven guys in shorts and T-shirts crowded around a color TV in dorm room 511, a spare cement cubicle decorated with three metal bunkbeds and yesterday's laundry. 
Nine student "shareholders" had bought the TV last month in anticipation of just such an occasion, and now hoots and jeers filled the air.
"Aya, that Malone he plays dirty."
"Nice ball. 
Go Rodman!"
"They're losing with three minutes to go. 
I can't stand it. 
Hit me with a hammer!"
Minutes later, half a world away, the Chicago Bulls clinched their sixth National Basketball Association championship with a final basket with only five seconds to play. 
The students jumped to their feet and began a refrain: "Qiao Dan, Qiao Dan, Qiao Dan."
Qiao Dan, of course, is Michael Jordan. 
Sure, Bill Clinton, President of the world's most powerful nation, is about to visit China. 
But to the Chinese, Michael Jordan remains America's king.
Mr. Clinton's state visit this month has brought out citizens' interest in all things American, from books to clothes to movie stars. 
But these all seem like passing fancies compared to the intense passion that Chinese, especially young Chinese, have developed for Michael Jordan and American basketball.
"Michael Jordan is much more famous than Clinton here," said Cheng Qian, 20, a Bulls fan and shareholder in the TV set who is a management major at Beijing University.
The Chinese have named him kongzhong feiren -- "space flier."
In the last week, businessmen, retired teachers, students and government officials have all paused to watch him, live on state-run television, as he led the Chicago Bulls to their 4-2 series victory over the Utah Jazz.
When Beijing Meilande Information Company recently asked 1,000 Chinese to name the best-known Americans ever, Michael Jordan came in second, trailing Thomas Edison by just a few percentage points. 
Behind him were Albert Einstein, Mark Twain and Bill Gates.
On the sidewalks of Jianguomenwai Avenue, vendors sell Michael Jordan posters. 
In department stores, Michael Jordan books and calendars sit beside those featuring Hong Kong movie stars and the late Chairman Mao.
"Of all American things, basketball is the most popular," said Li Fa, a junior, who could not join the crowd in 511 because he is a Jazz fan. 
"Everyone knows Michael Jordan."
State television began broadcasting prerecorded N.B.A. games in the early 1990's, and recently switched to live broadcasts. 
Today, Chinese viewers had three opportunities to see the final playoff game, which the Bulls won 87-86. 
The first was live at 7:30 A.M., then a taped game at 9 A.M. for late risers, and a replay at 9 P.M.
Chinese are hard pressed to say why they so adore the Bulls and Michael Jordan, who scored 45 points in the final game and was named Most Valuable Player.
"I don't know -- because of his skill, and because he alone carries half of the Chicago team," said Li Qixing, 20, another of the TV's shareholders.
American basketball is certainly more colorful than the home-grown variant, where the People's Liberation Army's August 1 team (named for the day the Army was founded) is the reigning champion. 
In skill and in entertainment value, Chinese players are no match for the likes of Dennis Rodman, who played the game with much of his hair dyed green.
Said Han Bai, a junior, sitting on his bunk bed in jeans and a T-shirt, "I couldn't accept this from a Chinese player, but he's an American so we expect it."
And American sportscasts have other attactions.
The students who gathered in 511 on this steamy morning, ooohed when they saw Leonardo DiCaprio, star of "Titanic," sitting at courtside. 
And, in a room full of male college juniors, the Jazz's cheerleaders, dancing in black leotards, got the thumbs up as well. 
Heads nodded in approval as Cheng Qian opined, "In this way, the Jazz are better than the Bulls."

file: Kou Qiu, Jordan! Slam Dunk! Pee-ow Liang!.txt
text:
ï»¿
"PEE-OW Liang!"
So the TV announcers say in China when Michael Jordan does his thing on the basketball court. 
And he is doing it, and they are saying it, to a growing audience of excited viewers all over China. 
("Pee-ow Liang!" means "Pretty!")
China's hottest American import is professional basketball, and Jordan and his Chicago Bulls are the flavor of the moment. 
Even if the television commentary by announcers is still rudimentary -- they don't yet have an equivalent for "nothing but net," and repeat "pee-ow liang!" all game long -- fan enthusiasm more than makes up for it.
"We're all hoping the Bulls can win 70 games this year," said Xing Tian, 17, who is the captain of her high school basketball team. 
"We want to see them break the record."
As Miss Xing knows, the Bulls need 19 more wins to be the first team in the National Basketball Association to win 70 games in a season. 
The team won Friday, although Jordan bruised his knee and elbow but vowed in last night's game.
Jackets emblazoned with "Chicago Bulls" have become fashionable here, and counterfeiters are churning out imitations. 
Sporting goods stores display posters of N.B.A. stars like Shaquille O'Neal and Charles Barkley rather than any of China's few basketball stars, who aren't that bad. 
The national men's basketball team has won 10 of the last 11 Asian championships.
State television is driving the craze. 
Miss Xing said she and her friends watch the weekly games -- two on weeknights and one on Saturday morning. 
"It's by far the most exciting thing on television," she said.
But the fervor isn't limited to children, many of whom grow up playing basketball in the schoolyard. 
A mention of "Chee-ow Dan," as Jordan is known in China, brings out smiles on adults as well.
"Everyone knows Jordan.

file: OBSERVATORY.txt
text:
ï»¿
Aggressive Crickets
What makes the elephant charge his tusk,
In the misty mist or the dusky dusk?
What makes the muskrat guard his musk?
Courage!
For the Cowardly Lion, who posed those questions in "The Wizard of Oz," aggressive behavior was a function of just one thing, which he sorely lacked. 
Scientists, however, know that it is not that simple, and indeed, what makes animals aggressive is not fully understood.
Now German and American researchers, writing in Nature, have provided new insight into aggression, at least among one species. 
What puts the fight in crickets?
Not courage, the researchers say, but flight.
Cricket fighting was a royal sport in ancient China and has persisted in some Chinese cities and in Chinese communities elsewhere. 
Gamblers bet on whether their insect will prevail in a fight that involves fencing with antennas, locking mandibles and wrestling. 
The losing cricket retreats, usually losing its will to fight.
But, as the gamblers know, a defeated cricket can regain its aggressiveness if it is shaken in cupped hands and thrown into the air a few times.
The scientists studied this effect, showing that it was not dependent on how long the insects were in the air, and not transitory -- aggressiveness remained restored for hours. 
Other stressful activity, like being tumbled in a rotating tube or walking in a wind, had no effect.
The researchers suggest that the specific motor pattern of flying produces some kind of command in the nervous system that resets aggression in the brain.
Â 
Tiniest Chemical Sensor
Nanotubes, those cylindrical molecules of carbon atoms, are steadily becoming much more than just a laboratory curiosity, as researchers develop potential applications for them.
One of the latest possible uses for nanotubes is as tiny chemical sensors. 
Researchers at Stanford report in the journal Science that they have used nanotubes to detect minute amounts of gases quickly and at room temperature.
The researchers used a single-walled nanotube, one in which just a single layer of carbon atoms forms the cylinder walls. 
These nanotubes are on the order of a billionth of a meter wide, and about three-millionths of a meter long. 
The structure of the molecule is such that it acts like a semiconductor if a charge is placed across it. 
This quality is what makes it useful as a sensor.
The researchers found that the electrical resistance of the nanotubes increased or decreased greatly when exposed to small amounts of nitrogen dioxide or ammonia. 
Nitrogen dioxide is found in car exhaust, among other sources, and gaseous ammonia is toxic, so tiny devices capable of detecting these gases would serve a real need.
The nanotubes were more sensitive than existing sensors. 
They also operated at room temperature. 
Most sensors currently used require heating to at least 400 degrees Fahrenheit.
Â 
The Mighty Nanotube
Before sensors or other devices based on nanotubes can be produced commercially, more has to be learned about the basic properties of these molecules. 
Scientists at Washington University in St. Louis have taken a step in that direction, determining for the first time the force needed to break one by stretching.
The study, reported in Science, used multiwalled nanotubes consisting of 10 to 40 single-walled tubes nested inside each other. 
The stretching occurs inside a scanning electron microscope, and the electron beam is used to fuse the ends of the nanotube to tiny cantilever tips that do the stretching.
The scientists said the force needed to break the nanotube was many times greater than would be required to break a similar-sized structure of steel, if it were possible to create one. 
Next up for the researcher: to break a single-walled tube.

text:

Forty of China's 300 Olympic athletes have withdrawn from the Summer Games, seven of them rowers who failed blood tests at home indicating that they were using performance-enhancing drugs, Olympic officials said today.
Favored to become the host city for the 2008 Summer Games, Beijing is apparently being extremely careful to avoid another doping scandal like those that tarnished the accomplishments of its swimmers in recent years. 
There has also been skepticism about the stunning achievements of China's distance runners in the early 1990's.
It was not known whether the other 33 withdrawals were related to drugs, Sydney Olympic officials stressed. 
Milton Cockburn, a spokesman for the Sydney Olympic Organizing Committee, said the withdrawals came after a request that countries pare down their teams or find other housing because the 10,400 available beds could not accommodate every athlete in the Olympic village.
The withdrawal of the seven rowers appears to indicate that the implementation of blood-testing procedures for the first time at these Sydney Games is having some deterrent effect on athletes in endurance sports who may look to cheat by illicitly trying to increase their oxygen-carrying capacity.
The International Olympic Committee last week approved testing for erythropoietin, or EPO, a synthetic version of a naturally occurring hormone that stimulates the production of red blood cells and is believed to be widely used in such endurance sports as distance running, cycling, swimming and rowing.
"People are now convinced there is a test, that the I.O.C. is prepared to apply it and nobody wants to send athletes to the Games that are going to get caught and disgraced," said Dick Pound, an I.O.C. vice president from Montreal who is head of the World Anti-Doping Agency, created by the I.O.C. in the wake of the EPO scandal at the 1998 Tour de France.

Steroid use is also so sophisticated that topical gels can be flushed from the system in a matter of hours. 
But the EPO test may deter cheaters and encourage athletes who do not cheat that the playing field is being made more level, Pound said.
"I don't want to be too superlative, but this is a terrific sign," Pound said in an interview this morning. 
"You end up with a double benefit."
The I.O.C. is conducting 2,100 out-of-competition tests in Sydney, including 300 tests for EPO. 
Unannounced, out-of-competition tests are considered the only reliable way to catch cheaters. 
The EPO test is a combination of a French urine test that can detect direct use of the drug for 2 or 3 days and an Australian blood test that detects indirect use of EPO. 
Privately, I.O.C. scientists say they are concerned about whether the tests will withstand legal scrutiny. 
But the test can be just as valuable if it discourages athletes from using EPO for fear they might be caught, Pound said.
The Chinese rowers, who included Zhang Xiuyun, a gold medalist in the women's single scull at a World Cup race in Zurich, Switzerland, last June, were presumably subjected in China to a hematocrit test that showed high red-blood cell counts, an indirect measure of the use of EPO, Pound said.
Liu Jianyong, secretary general of the Chinese rowing federation, said the rowers had withdrawn to "protect their health" -- a euphemism often used in drug cases.
China has publicly stated its determination to conduct more vigilant drug-testing procedures after being embarrassed repeatedly in recent years. 
Unlike the former East Germany, which operated a state-sponsored system of doping, China's doping appears to be conducted largely by individual coaches, according to American coaches and drug experts. 
Its female swimmers and distance runners have been far less dominant since the mid-1990's.
More than 30 Chinese swimmers were caught using drugs in the last decade, including 7 at the 1994 Asian Games.

"
"This won't do them any harm" for 2008, he said.

Eight years after she won the first Olympic race-walking competition for women as a Chinese athlete, Yueling Chen hoped to win another medal, this time as a United States citizen, at the 2000 Summer Games in Sydney, Australia.
However, China has protested her participation as an American, and given the citizenship requirements of the Olympics, it appears that Chen will have to watch the Sydney Games as a spectator.
Chen, who competed for China as Chen Yueling but prefers the Western listing of her name, obtained her American citizenship on April 12. 
Last month in Sacramento, she finished second in the 20-kilometer (12.4-mile) walk at the United States Olympic track and field trials, which conditionally qualified her for the Sydney Games in September.
However, an athlete who has competed in the Games for one country must wait three years to compete for another country after gaining citizenship in the new nation. 
This rule is meant to prevent Olympic athletes from playing musical chairs with their citizenship.
A waiver can be granted, and frequently has been, but the Chinese track-and-field federation has declined to issue one. 
Tuesday, without explanation, the Chinese Olympic Committee notified the United States Olympic Committee that it supported the Chinese track federation's decision.
The International Olympic Committee indicated yesterday that it would not get involved in this or other similar cases, saying it was a matter for the Olympic committees of the United States and China to decide. 
"We don't arbitrate these cases," said Franklin Servan-Schreiber, an I.O.C. spokesman.
Barring I.O.C. intervention, the case appears to be closed, said Mike Moran, a spokesman for the U.S.O.C. 
Earlier this year, even after United States Olympic officials traveled to Havana to plead their case, Cuba denied to grant a waiver to Angel Perez, a canoe-kayaker who had become a United States citizen.The I.O.C. did not intercede in that case.
"I think that's the end of it," Moran said last night. 
"I don't think we have any wiggle room."
One senior I.O.C. official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, left some small opening, saying that China might be wise to reconsider its position, considering that Beijing is bidding on the 2008 Summer Games and might not want to anger the United States. 
Beijing lost by two votes to Sydney to become the host city of the 2000 Summer Games.
"It would be useful for the Chinese to approve that transfer," the I.O.C. official said. 
"America is a powerful country and can always be helpful. 
People remember things like this. 
Good faith and good form shown when things are delicate could make a difference. 
Everything is important when you are bidding."
The Chinese and the American Olympic committees enjoy cordial relations, Moran said. 
Earlier this year, the Chinese granted waivers for three athletes who had become American citizens, two table tennis players and a badminton player, he said. 
The difference is that Chen has represented China in the Olympics and the others have not, Moran said.
Chen is the first Chinese woman to win a gold medal in track and field, and is perhaps the most successful Chinese athlete ever to attempt to compete for another country, which may explain China's reluctance to grant her a waiver.
"She is clearly higher profile because of her past success," Moran said. 
"That may be it."
Now living in Escondido, Calif., the 27-year-old Chen said that China's refusal to let her compete for the United States was "unbelievably unfair to me."
In a statement issued through her agent, Derek Boosey, Chen recalled the words of the French baron, Pierre de Coubertin, who founded the modern Olympics and said the most important thing was to compete.
"That's all I want to do," Chen said. 
"I just want to compete."
Chinese Olympic officials could not be reached for comment.
At the 1992 Summer Games in Barcelona, Spain, Chen won the inaugural 10-kilometer (6.2-mile) walk for women in a controversial decision after the Russian walker, Alina Ivanova, crossed the line first, only to be disqualified for technical violations. 
Race walkers must keep one foot on the ground at all times. 
Three years earlier, Chen had set a world record in the 10-kilometer walk in 43 minutes 52.1 seconds. 
After she won in Barcelona in 44:52, a statue of Chen was erected in her home town of Taeling, in Liaoning province.
In 1993, Chen immigrated to the United States, receiving a green card as an alien with extraordinary ability, and Chinese athletic officials did not protest the move, she said.

So did the pairs of middle-aged men and women in shorts or sweatsuits doing paddle-to-paddle combat, engaging in forehand slams and backhand chops to the applause of well-dressed onlookers. 
So, against that backdrop, did Henry Kissinger.
But to those who gathered there Thursday evening to celebrate one of the more remarkable chapters in diplomatic history, the scene was a perfectly apt reminder that in 1971, an American table-tennis team visited China and thawed relations between two stubborn superpowers that had been frozen in rigid enmity for more than 20 years.
The American visit (which the Chinese reciprocated by coming here a year later), brought two cultures face to face for the first time in a generation, and not without mutual astonishment. 
But more important, it initiated the era of what became known as "Ping-Pong diplomacy."
Three months after the 15 American table-tennis players and officials returned home, Mr. Kissinger, then President Richard M. Nixon's national security adviser, traveled to Beijing (the city formerly known as Peking) for talks with the Chinese Prime Minister, Zhou Enlai. 
That October, the Communist Government of the mainland took China's seat in the United Nations from the Nationalist Government on Taiwan; the following year, President Nixon made his own celebrated trip to China, meeting with Zhou and the Communist Party chairman, Mao Zedong.
At the United Nations Thursday night, Mr. Kissinger, speaking in his signature deadpan rumble, recounted for the 200 or so guests -- who included several table-tennis luminaries and Tricia Nixon Cox, one of the former President's daughters -- a little of the history in which he played so central a role.
By the time the Chinese invited the American team, he said, he and President Nixon were already involved in back-channel negotiations to hold talks between the two nations.
Indeed, Zhou had already extended the invitation for an American emissary to visit Beijing, but the Americans had been dilatory in responding. 
The Chinese, he suggested, must have thought the Americans needed prodding, so they took advantage of the fact that the American table-tennis team was playing in a tournament in nearby Japan to send a signal.
"I think Zhou Enlai thought Westerners were slower than the Chinese in mental perception, and didn't think we had understood the message," Mr. Kissinger said. 
"So just as we were drafting a response to the message we had received, we heard he had invited the Ping-Pong team."
Beyond the history being celebrated, Thursday's event, which was organized by the National Committee on United States-China relations, was an occasion for laughter and reminiscing, if not exactly nostalgia; it was more like amazement at what can transpire in a mere quarter-century.
"Everything was different from anything I'd ever seen," said Tim Boggan, an American player, recalling his arrival in Beijing. 
After a wine reception and a few speeches, Mr. Boggan had changed from a jacket and tie into a sweatsuit, and was jogging in place in anticipation of playing a mixed-doubles exhibition. 
"The streets were different," he said. 
"The food was different. 
The people, of course, were different. 
The bicycles were different."
Connie Sweeris, an American who also played in an exhibition Thursday, was 23 when she went to China in 1971; she said she had been basically unaware of the significance of the visit until it was over.
"When we came out, it was news all over the world," she said. 
Ms. Sweeris, who now runs a preschool in Grand Rapids, Mich., still remembers that at dinner one night, out of politeness more than inclination, she drank a toast with a beverage apparently popular in China.
"After I drank, they poured some out of the glass, and lit it up," she said. 
"That was interesting."
To this day, she has no idea what she had been drinking.
The Chinese, more than the Americans, remembered apprehensions.
"I knew they would be unlike any other games I'd ever played," said Zheng Minzhi, 51, speaking through an interpreter. 
"I knew their significance and my responsibilities. 
I knew I was not only there to play, but more important, to achieve what cannot be achieved through proper diplomatic channels."
She had also been nervous. 
"I knew nothing about the country or the people," said Ms. Zheng, who now runs a cultural exchange program in Shanghai. 
"What would I say to them?
What would they say to me?
But all these concerns vanished as soon as we met."
It was in late March 1971, when both the American and Chinese teams were playing in the world championships in Nagoya, Japan, that the Chinese extended their surprise invitation. 
Barely two weeks later, the nine American players, four officials and two spouses were in Beijing. 
It seems today like an unremarkable gesture, but it was a landmark moment. 
Relations between the two nations had been nearly stone silent since 1949, when Mao and his Communists drove the Nationalist followers of Chiang Kai-shek from the Chinese mainland.
"As I told the U.S. 
Table Tennis association officials at the time," said Bill Cunningham, who in 1971 was serving in the American Embassy in Tokyo as a "China watcher," " 'the number of people who are going with you to China is greater than the aggregate number of Americans who have been to China since 1950.'
"
The visit was not without its political and cultural clashes. 
One member of the American team, who had been born in South Korea, decided, out of loyalty to his homeland and family, not to make the trip. 
John Tannehill, a 19-year-old from Ohio, declared, much to the embarrassment of the United States, that Mao was "the greatest moral and intellectual leader in the world."
And Glenn Cowan, a long-haired Californian, also 19, who walked China's streets in tie-dyed blue jeans, asked Zhou what he thought of American hippies.
"Youth wants to seek out the truth, and out of this search various forms of change are bound to come," Zhou replied.
But there was little to clash over on Thursday. 
And indeed, Mr. Kissinger, a longtime advocate of American trade with China, declared during his remarks that "all we need now is a Ping-Pong team to give the enterprise a human touch and break down the encrusted debate."
Of course, the Chinese, still the world's best players, have never been much at risk at the Ping-Pong table with the Americans. 
Most of those who visited China in 1971 admitted that even though they lost their matches -- which were against local teams, not the national team -- they felt the Chinese had taken it easy on them, letting them win a few games.
Thursday night, after several good-humored exhibition matches between the older rivals, four members of the current Chinese national team, including Deng Yaping, the women's world champion, and Liu Guoliang, the 1996 men's Olympic champion, stepped up to the Ping-Pong table. 
The speed and power of the play was ratcheted up by several orders of magnitude.
The oohs and aahhs became more audible, just as they had been in 1972, when the Chinese team made its return visit to the United States and played Ping-Pong at the United Nations. 
The New York Times covered the event then, saying "the most sustained applause and loudest shouts of admiration were during the games the Chinese played against one another."
Some things don't change.

file: SOCCER_A Narrow Victory Leaves Questions for U.S. Women.txt
text:

With the women's World Cup approaching in June, the United States appeared to have lost its scoring touch and any certainty that it was still head and shoulders above every other team in the tournament.
But after missing numerous opportunities tonight, the Americans rescued a 2-1 exhibition victory over China two minutes into extra time on a rebound shot by Tisha Venturini.
Mia Hamm fired a low cross from the right side that Han Wenxia, the Chinese goalkeeper, poked away. 
Venturini, who had entered in the 90th minute as a substitute, pounced on the ricochet and punched the ball into the net from seven yards out, awakening a quiet crowd of 15,257 at Hersheypark Stadium.
"I hit it as hard as I could across the goal and Tisha made this unbelievable run from midfield," Hamm said.
Venturini said, "You know Mia is going to get there, so I just kept running."
Tonight's friendly was seen by many as a potential preview of the World Cup final, scheduled for July 10 at the Rose Bowl in Pasadena, Calif. 
The teams will meet again Sunday in an exhibition at Giants Stadium.
The Americans, who lost by 2-1 to China in Portugal's Algarve Cup last month, dominated play in the first half but continued to struggle with putting the ball into the net. 
Cindy Parlow pounded a shot off the post in the seventh minute, then failed to lift a chip shot over Han.
In the 12th minute, Hamm made a brilliant feint to her left, moved to her right around a Chinese defender but shot the ball just wide left from 17 yards out.
Hamm is considered the world's best player, and with 104 career goals, she is only 3 shy of the women's career record. 
But it has now been six games since she has scored a goal. 
But she set up both American goals tonight.
In the 20th minute, the American defender Brandi Chastain won a tackle near midfield and caught the Chinese defense too far forward as she put the ball through to Hamm, who sprinted free down the left flank. 
Wen Lirong had no choice but to drag Hamm down in the penalty area.
Michelle Akers took the penalty kick and drilled the ball low and to the left. 
Han, a substitute Chinese goalie who was playing in only her seventh international match, guessed correctly and got her hands on the ball, but she could not keep it out of the net.
China, which failed to get a shot on goal until the 24th minute, tied the game in the 59th minute when forward Sun Wen hooked a free kick into the net from about 25 yards out.
The Americans seemed headed for a draw as Hamm then missed twice on free kicks, but her late blast left Venturini open for the game winner.

file: Sports of The Times_Final Game Owes Great Debt to China.txt
text:
ï»¿
EVER since the American organizers took out their indelible-ink pens and plotted the inexorable march from sea to shining sea, there were chauvinistic and realistic expectations that the Yanks would win this 1999 Women's World Cup.
Hardly anybody could have predicted the sudden hysteria for this appealing bunch of Johnettes and Paulettes and Georgettes and Ringoettes, but there surely was the assumption that the combination of home cooking and summer weather and loyal home crowds would make a difference.
Now there is reason to think the Chinese could spurt right past the Americans this afternoon at the Rose Bowl. 
Then, given America's fascination with winning, what happens to all the brave talk about marketing these charismatic athletes?
Still, if the Chinese should win today, they would merely be recapturing command of an event they initiated.
That's true. 
Like many of the items you bring back from the mall, the Women's World Cup carries a label that says, "Made in China."
If there had not been 65,000 fans at the stadium in Guangzhou on Nov. 
30, 1991, there very likely would not be 90,000 fans at the Rose Bowl today.
The Chinese also invented pasta, even though Carla Overbeck, the United States' co-captain, and her chef-husband, Greg, had to slip packages of pasta ("and spices, and I carried a wheel of Parmesan cheese," Overbeck recalled) with her gear back in 1991.
The American women were really pioneers back then, catching up on a sport that was played mainly by women from northern Europe.
"Honestly, we had no idea," Overbeck said this week, on a practice field surrounded by squealing fans and protected by a squad of motorcycle police.
"We had never been to a big tournament, and it wasn't even called a World Cup," Overbeck added.
Overbeck and her husband were not sure what the menu would be like in Guangzhou, so they carried packaged foodstuff with them.
"They wouldn't let Greg cook," Overbeck recalled, "so he had to draw diagrams and point how he wanted it done. 
But toward the end, they let him cook."
The women were glad to have a taste of home. 
(In this strange hybrid land of America, Italian cuisine is home cooking.) But they had no complaints about the ambience.
"We stayed at the White Swan Hotel, a five-star hotel," Joy Fawcett said. 
"We brought peanut butter, and we got by, just as I'm sure they're getting by over here."
Michelle Akers said: "I remember it was the first time we had ever seen outdoor food markets. 
Some of the food choices were pretty unusual. 
Sure, I tasted them, after taking a picture of them first."
The women had enjoyed modest crowds and celebrity in college, but 1991 was their first experience in an international tournament.
"I had to convince my dad to come over," recalled Julie Foudy. 
"He came to our hotel, and there were huge banners and flower displays, and he said, 'I can't believe the magnitude of this.'
It was unfortunate the Chinese lost in the quarterfinals, but it was a great tournament."
The Americans beat Norway in the final in front of that crowd of 65,000, at that point believed to be the largest ever to see a women's sporting event. 
The Swedish organizers in 1995 had a much more modest scale -- the United States lost in the semifinals to Norway in front of little more than 2,000 -- and now the American organizers have exceeded their own grandiose dreams.
"It was great to see 65,000 in China," said Lauren Gregg, an assistant American coach, "but most of them were factory workers who were let off from work."
Now there is the matter of the 1999 final. 
The Chinese were stung by their early loss in 1991 in front of their fans, but they just did not have the sophisticated techniques. 
Today, they do. 
They destroyed Norway, 5-0, in the semifinal last Sunday. 
Their passing is superb, their attack aggressive, their defense coordinated, and their goalkeeping confident.
In a country where most eyes were glazing over at talk of women's soccer only a few weeks ago, there is a touch of midsummer madness for this event. 
But would one loss to China turn the entire experience into a Pet Rock or a Hula-Hoop?
Up to now, the greatest long-standing United States women's team was a volleyball team, led by the talented Flo Hyman, that lived in makeshift training camps and made grueling international swings to prepare for the 1984 Olympics in Los Angeles.
At the time, I might have predicted that women's volleyball, with its emphasis on grace and teamwork, would become the most popular American women's team sport. 
But the Americans lost the gold-medal match to -- ah, but you guessed it -- China. 
And whatever happened to women's volleyball?
Women's soccer is not going away. 
Some young women in the crowd with their "Hamm" and "Scurry" shirts are going to be playing for the United States in the next century. 
They will be competing with the heirs to Gao and Sun in a sport that already owes a great debt to China.

file: Sports of The Times_Now Beijing Must Wait 4 More Years.txt
text:
ï»¿
CHINA is not going anywhere. 
There it sits, one fifth of the world's population, hurtling toward the next century, the next millenium, when it will surely be host to the Summer Games, sooner rather than later. 
It is inevitable. 
It is China.
But Beijing will not hold the Games in the year 2000 because yesterday they were awarded to Sydney, Australia, a cosmopolitan city on the southern half of the world, close to Asia, and a very acceptable choice.
The apparent hard glares above the smiling mouths in the Chinese delegation suggested they were not amused by the voting by delegates to the International Olympic Committee. 
And they have every right to be upset.
Beijing led Sydney on three separate ballots, 32-30, 37-30 and 40-37, but could not muster an absolute majority. 
When Manchester was eliminated, the ballots tipped to Sydney, 45-43, which is how it works in the old Olympic game. 
It is called paying your dues.
Maybe the sun still hasn't totally set on the old Empire. 
Melbourne and Toronto were left behind in the last stampede to the obscure charms of Atlanta; now Manchester blocks Beijing until Sydney can gain a majority. 
And China could not count on any Communist-bloc votes these days; it is hard to imagine any eastern European delegates voting for their good buddies from Beijing.
China has come too far to slam the doors and windows shut, but it will be hard for China to save face by accepting the choice of Sydney as pragmatic rather than political. 
It is very soon after the brutal events in Tiananmen Square in 1989 and the world is well aware of thousands of dissidents in Chinese jails. 
Chinese officials did not help their cause by boasting there would be no demonstrations against the Games in the next seven years. 
As somebody once said in another context, they just don't get it.
But few of the delegates may have been swayed much by the recommendations by the United States Congress that China be passed over. 
And few delegates may have been moved by the passionate lobbying of groups like Human Rights Watch, which keep people alive and out of jails all over the world. 
By and large, people do not get to be delegates to the I.O.C. because of a preoccupation with human rights.
More to the point, the delegates often vote for creature comforts. 
Four years ago, this same group voted for a second-tier American city, Atlanta, for the 1996 Games, only 12 years after the Games in Los Angeles. 
There was no reason to go back to the United States so soon, except maybe Atlanta was in the right time zone for television and lobbied the hardest. 
Now Australia gets the Games, four years later.
Sydney surely has the infrastructure of a major first-world city -- the hotels, the phones, the arenas, the roads -- while Beijing was just describing how it would go about building them.
The delegates were left with a perfect out by the evaluation report on six bidding cities, delivered last July. 
Sydney had the highest marks because all events would be within 30 minutes of each other. 
Manchester and Berlin scored well, Brasilia failed, and Istanbul and Beijing were marginal. 
Those delegates on an inspection tour did not miss the point when Beijing shut down its furnaces in the middle of winter to try to clean up the murky air.
"It must be noted that China currently falls significantly below international standards," read the report on China's environment.
In some ways, it would have been brave to award the Games to China. 
I am not talking here from any anachronistic sentiments about the purity of the Olympic movement. 
The sneaker companies and the cola companies promote these Games for profit.
It would have been a practical statement to bring China just a little closer to the rest of the world. 
But there is no guarantee that holding the Games will purge any country of its ancient traditions. 
Witness the raping and killing in Sarajevo, where the 1984 Winter Games were held.
China has made huge strides in living standards in recent years. 
Its totalitarian government could probably have built the Olympic facilities in the next seven years, but what's the rush?
Chinese officials have already promised not to boycott the 1996 Games, and they would be foolish to even think of it. 
Besides, why are athletes asked to carry the burden of failed politics?
Why not tourists?
Why not companies pushing soft drinks or cigarettes?
Why not arms vendors?
With her female runners turning in incredible times, after a promising performance in Barcelona in 1992, China would be wise to show up in Atlanta and Sydney and take as many gold medals as it can, and make as many friends as it can. 
Play the game. 
Time is on China's side.

file: Sports of The Times_Two Great Rivalries In the Women_s Game.txt
text:
ï»¿
THIS summer's Women's World Cup gained instant credibility yesterday. 
This was apparent from the steamed looks on the faces of the American players, who discovered they can, in fact, lose on the green, green grass of home.
They had not lost in the United States in 50 games, but lose they did, 2-1, to China in a highly competitive exhibition that reminded everybody there are no Dream Teams this summer, no Charles Barkley whupping on the Angolans.
The American public and also the news media have not yet come to grips with this event -- 16 national teams coming to the United States in what will be the best-attended sports event held only for female athletes. 
The third Women's World Cup, from June 19 through July 10, gained a huge amount of respectability yesterday if only because it showed the United States is vulnerable, at least in the medal round.
The promoters have sold 325,000 tickets, aiming toward 475,000, and they can probably sell more tickets from bone-rattling hits like the ones that leveled Mia Hamm and Michelle Akers yesterday than from potential double-digit romps.
"China is the favorite right now," said Dr. Robert Contiguglia, the president of the United States Soccer Federation, shortly after China won the game three minutes into injury time.
Yesterday's crowd of 23,765 might have been bigger if prospective fans had not feared they had to watch the MetroStars first, like taking your medicine before a tasteful dinner. 
The locals lost to Tampa Bay, 1-0, probably not setting back Major League Soccer more than six or eight years.
The women promptly aired out the joint. 
China against the United States would be the best women's team rivalry in the world, except that Norway-United States got there first, and besides that, the Norwegians all speak English, so little gibes have built up, along with the bruises. 
China-United States, however, is getting there.
The Chinese were stunned at losing early in the first Women's World Cup, which was in their country in 1991, but time, as somebody once said, is on their side. 
They studied and traveled, and trained, and now they can play.
"They are so fast and so technical," said Hamm, who now has gone seven straight games without scoring. 
"That gave them the opportunity to win on a random clear."
The United States has still won 11 and lost 5 and tied 5 against China, with significant victories for the Summer Games gold medal in Georgia in 1996, and for the Goodwill Games title last summer. 
Then last month, China upended the Americans, 2-1, in the final of the prestigious Algarve tournament in Portugal.
There was another sign that the Yanks are not going to dominate their festival this summer. 
Last February, just after the draw for the World Cup, the United States lost, 2-1, to a group of world all-stars who had literally held one workout together the day before. 
It wasn't only feisty Linda Medalen of Norway playing traffic cop in the back four; it was emerging players from Japan and Nigeria and Canada giving what-for to the Americans.
Dynasties do wear out, like the Boston Celtics of the Bill Russell-K. 
C. Jones era, or the Islanders of the early 80's, the games and the miles adding up like dog years. 
But this is more a case of other nations catching up.
When the United States beat China, 2-1, last Thursday in Hershey, Pa., the Chinese played without their star goalkeeper, Gao Hong, who was said to be injured. 
Late in the game, the Yanks forced the play for a goal in the 92d minute.
"That's the way we are," said their coach, Tony DiCicco, yesterday. 
"They treat a tie as a loss."
They faced a loss yesterday when China's top scorer, Sun Wen, hammered a goal past Briana Scurry in the 14th minute.
"At halftime, Julie Foudy said: 'This is a test for us. 
It will show how we handle adversity,' " Hamm said later. 
"It didn't turn out the way we wanted, but we did come back."
They tied the game in the 58th minute when Cindy Parlow crossed the ball to Foudy, who made an intricate fake to her left, then waited for traffic to clear and smacked the ball past Gao, who played a terrific game.
"I only have short-term memory," Foudy said, still steamed after the game. 
"I can't remember the goal."
They could only remember how, on home turf, the Chinese swarmed around Hamm in extra time, then whacked the ball downfield, where a speedy Zhang Ouying burst past Carla Overbeck and Christie Pearce and put the ball under Scurry.
"Did we just lose that game?"
Foudy blurted into a television microphone a few seconds after the final whistle.
They did indeed lose. 
But the 1999 Women's World Cup was the biggest winner. 
Patriotism sells tickets, but parity sells even more.
