file: SWIMMING_New Accusations Aimed at Chinese Swimmers.txt
text:
ï»¿
Luggage belonging to a Chinese swimmer was seized yesterday by Australian custom officials who said it contained a substance labeled as human growth hormone. 
If the label is correct, the incident would reinforce the widely held belief that China's female swimmers have been using banned bodybuilding drugs.
Yuan Yuan, a breast-stroke swimmer who won a silver medal at the 1994 world championships, was part of a 29-person Chinese group flying from Beijing to Sydney to Perth for the world championships. 
The Australian customs service said a routine search of luggage in Sydney uncovered 13 vials packed in ice in a thermos flask. 
It said there were 13 more vials of a diluting fluid.
The spokesman said the vials, which were not declared, were clearly labeled in English as human somatropin, a human growth hormone that athletes have been known to use in place of anabolic steroids. 
All those drugs are banned by the International Olympic Committee and the international federations governing each Olympic sport, but there are no effective tests to detect the use of human growth hormone.
Athletes use the drugs to train more intensively, with a quicker recovery time. 
Used in conjunction with weight lifting and a high-protein diet, the drugs also promote muscle growth.
A laboratory analysis of the substance seized at the airport may be available today. 
The International Swimming Federation, known by its French initials as FINA, said it would have no comment until the vials had been analyzed. 
It also said it could not take action without proof that athletes had used illegal drugs.
It was unclear exactly who the vials belonged to, and there has been no official comment on the incident from Yuan or the Chinese swimming federation. 
Yuan told customs officers that the vials belonged to her coach. 
John Hawksworth, an Australian customs official, said a team coach said he packed the bag. 
A Chinese team official said Yuan was bringing in the substance for a friend in Australia.
Deryk Snelling, the national performance director for British swimming, said FINA should consider banning China from the championships, which began earlier this week. 
"It'll penalize a lot of people," he said, "but it's the only way they'll get the message."
Western swimming officials have insisted that despite denials by the Chinese, the rise of China's female swimmers in the 1990's is a result of illegal drug use. 
The reaction to the seizure in Australia was one of vindication.
"This time, they've been caught with their hands in the cookie jar," said Don Talbot, the Australian national coach.
"We dream of such moments," said Mark Schubert, an assistant coach of the United States team.
In last October's Chinese national championships, two world records were set and the women swam the year's fastest time in eight events, fueling suspicions that the Chinese were using banned substances. 
In 1994, the swimmers won 12 of the 16 gold medals in the world championships in Rome. 
Two months later, at the Asian Games in Hiroshima, Japan, seven Chinese female swimmers tested positive for the use of anabolic steroids.
In all, 23 Chinese swimmers have tested positive since 1990 for using steroids. 
Officials from other nations demanded that FINA establish out-of-competition testing, which it did. 
Shi Tianshu, the leader of the Chinese team at Perth, said his federation had conducted more than 100 out-of-competition tests in the last two months, more than 650 in the last year, with no positive results.
On Tuesday, Shi said his country was clean on the drug issue. 
"We compare with any nation in the fight against drugs," he said.
Hawksworth said the confiscated material was found by accident. 
He said one passenger on the plane fit a narcotics profile. 
That person's baggage was inspected and nothing turned up. 
Yuan's bags were on the same trolley, and, Hawksworth said, "We found the stuff."
A journalist from Hong Kong Star Television identified Yuan's coach as Zhou Ming and said he remained in Sydney after the vials were discovered. 
After questioning, the others went on to Perth, where they learned that 12 teammates who arrived two days before had been tested for drugs after practice that morning.
It was a bad day all around for FINA. 
It had lifted the world-championship accreditation of Winfried Leopold, the German coach, after he admitted he had given banned drugs to athletes in East Germany. 
Yesterday, an Australian court ordered the credential restored.
And in an interview to be published today in the German newspaper Chemnitz Morgenpost, Petra Kind-Schneider, a 1980 Olympic swimming champion for East Germany, said she had heart and liver problems as a result of years of drug use. 
She said she started taking drugs just after her 14th birthday and was told to take blue pills four times a day, but that no one told her they contained anabolic steroids.

file: SWIMMING_Thompson_s Two Golds Cap Fine U.S. Showing.txt
text:
ï»¿
The United States won three of four events today on the final day of the Pan Pacific swimming championships and emerged as the top team in the first major test of the "fast" pool where Olympic events will be swum next year.
Twelve world records were set during the 8-day, 12-nation meet at the Sydney International Aquatic Center.
The American team -- led by the sprinter Jenny Thompson and the backstrokers Lenny Krayzelburg and Brooke Bennett, who among them won 11 medals -- edged out the host nation in medals, 35-32, and in points, 391-372.
However, the Australians, led by Ian Thorpe, Michael Klim and Susie O'Neill, matched the American gold medal tally of 13. 
The last time Australia bested the United States in total medals at a swimming competition was in 1956, at the Olympics in Melbourne.
Today, for the first time in these championships, no world records were set. 
Thompson earned her fifth and sixth gold medals of the meet, winning the 50-meter freestyle and swimming the butterfly leg in the women's medley relay. 
The American men's medley relay also won.
In the men's 1,500 freestyle, 19-year-old Grant Hackett of Australia won in 14 minutes 45.60 seconds, the second-fastest time ever.
The brightest star of the championships was Penny Heyns, the 24-year-old South African breast-stroke specialist who lives in Canada. 
Heyns set four world records at distances from 50 to 200 meters, bringing her haul of world records to eight in the last six weeks.
Swimming's oldest record survived the onslaught. 
Mary T. Meagher's 2:05.96 in the 200 butterfly, set in 1981, withstood a strong challenge last Thursday by O'Neill, the defending Olympic champion. 
O'Neill, 26, fell 0.64 of a second short.
However, the second butterfly record Meagher set in 1981 was finally broken. 
Thompson, 26, clipped five-hundredths of a second off Meagher's 18-year-old record in the 100 butterfly.
Meagher, now 34, said: "I knew this day would come. 
This now means that a part of my journey in swimming is over. 
There is a new record holder, and someone can go after Jenny."
The Chinese team was conspicuous for being almost invisible. 
Chinese swimmers qualified for only one final and finished last in that.
China originally named 20 swimmers for the meet, but sent only five. 
The reason given by Chinese authorities was the "conflicting domestic schedule" of the All-China Games in October.
The coach of the United States women's team, Richard Quick, and Australia's national coach, Don Talbot, were among officials here who expressed suspicions of the Chinese explanation. 
A series of Chinese female swimmers have been suspended for using performance-enhancing drugs in recent years.
However, the president of the Australian Swimming Federation, Terry Gathercole, said he was encouraged by the fact that in the last year Chinese officials had reported 10 instances of the use of banned substances by their own swimmers. 
"This indicates that China is trying" to act on the problem, he said.

file: SWIMMING_U.S. Ban of Chinese Swimmers Criticized.txt
text:
ï»¿
Officials of swimming's world governing body yesterday criticized the United States, Canada and Australia for banning China from a pre-Olympic meet this summer in Atlanta.
In light of seven recent positive drug tests among Chinese swimmers, including two world champions, the three aquatic powers voted on Sunday in Honolulu to prohibit China from swimming in the Pan Pacific Championships in August. 
The Pan Pacs, as they are known, will serve as a test event for the 1996 Summer Games in Atlanta. 
Japan cast the lone dissenting vote among Pan-Pac charter members.
Yesterday, two officials of FINA, the sport's governing body, said it was premature to ban China from the meet. 
Last week, FINA announced plans to control the drug problem in Chinese swimming.
First, it will send a commission to China in March to investigate the involvement of swimmers, coaches, doctors and team officials in the use of banned substances. 
Second, FINA will substantially increase the number of out-of-competition drug tests administered in 1995. 
Third, a special congress will be convened in Rio de Janeiro in December to impose stricter penalties for doping.
United States swimming officials have called for greater vigilance since the Chinese women won 12 of 16 gold medals at the world championships in Rome last September. 
While they applaud the latest steps taken by FINA, American officials said, the ban was necessary because harsher penalties for drug use would not be implemented in time for the Pan Pacific Championships.
"We believe that this is not premature; it is based on substantial evidence that there is some kind of structured or organized doping for sports in the People's Republic of China," said Ray Essick, the executive director of the United States Swimming Federation. 
"Until we are given absolute proof that this will no longer take place, or until appropriate rules or sanctions are in place from FINA to deal with it, we're not interested in having our athletes compete in an unfair competition."
Gunnar Werner, the honorary secretary of FINA, called the ban of Chinese athletes from the Pan Pacs "regrettable."
Cornel Marculescu, the director of FINA, said in a telephone interview: "Perhaps this is not the best way to solve these problems. 
FINA has already taken strong actions against doping."
Officials from FINA and the International Olympic Committee also made it clear yesterday that they have no intention of banning all Chinese swimmers from the 1996 Summer Games. 
The seven Chinese swimmers suspended after the Asian Games in Japan last fall will be ineligible, however, including the world champions Lu Bin and Yang Aihua. 
All seven tested positive for the anabolic steroid dihydrotestosterone, commonly known as DHT.
"Excluding a whole nation or a delegation because some athletes, or some in their entourage, break rules, I don't think would be an appropriate measure," Francois Carrard, director general of the I.O.C., said in a telephone interview from Lausanne, Switzerland.

file: SYDNEY 2000_ GYMNASTICS_After 40 Years of Expectation, Mighty Chinese Come Through.txt
text:
ï»¿
The last event of the night was unfolding when the usually stoic Chinese gymnasts tilted their heads to the rafters like dust bowl survivors welcoming the first raindrop.
Suddenly, there was relief. 
Revealing untraditional emotion, they jumped around in a huddle on the side of the podium once they realized the 40-year spell that had left their mighty teams with nothing but Olympic consolation prizes had come to an end.
Tonight, the team gold medal in men's gymnastics belonged to China for the first time. 
Almost giddy, the Chinese gymnasts floated onto the podium at the Dome and saluted the collection of fans waving their country's flag in the seats. 
A moment later, several of the gymnasts glanced down at their priceless medallions, stared at every detail and held them in their palms, not wanting to let go.
"We have worked hard for several generations," Coach Huang Yubin said through a translator. 
"We have fought for this for 40 years. 
We think we should taste the fruits of the Champagne."
In every pocket of China, there was cause for celebration. 
After five world championships, but three Olympic silver medals since 1984, China could go home having conquered all the heavy expectations. 
Instead of buckling under the Olympic pressure as they had in the past, the Chinese thrived on the challenge, finishing a dominant 1.613 points ahead of the silver medalists from Ukraine and 2.062 points in front of the bronze medal winners from Russia.
"We were under some pressure," Huang acknowledged, "but this was our best chance today."
This was the Americans' opportunity, too. 
This was their moment to separate themselves from their position as background scenery to the popular United States women's program, and grab their first medal since their 1984 gold medal heyday. 
After their fourth-place position in the preliminaries, the Americans had a bronze medal on their minds.
But at the same time the Chinese began their celebration on one side of the arena, a snapshot of the United States' collapsible performance was developing on the horizontal bar. 
In need of a miracle as they entered the event, languishing in fifth position after five of the six apparatus, the Americans watched with horror as their top two gymnasts crashed to the mat during their routines.
The 17-year-old Paul Hamm blew his usually calm cover and fell twice on a difficult release move. 
Then, the team's star, Blaine Wilson, swung into his release move but could only swipe at the bar with his fingertips as he fell into the padding.
With that, the Americans' fate as the fifth-place team was sealed. 
In a sign of their inability to show progress, their finish was the same as it was in 1996. 
Once again, the American men couldn't find a consistent leader to guide them through the team competition. 
Wilson, the five-time national champion, wasn't up to it. 
Even on his signature event, the still rings, he wowed everyone with his strength moves but took a big step back on his dismount.
Although he scored a 9.7 on the vault and a 9.775 on the parallel bars, the Americans needed Wilson to be spectacular in every area. 
The horizontal bar, and his score of 9.050, only punctuated a disappointing night for him.
"We wouldn't be where we are without Blaine; he has carried us for a long time," said the three-time Olympian John Roethlisberger, who finished his gymnastics career with a 9.7 on the horizontal bar. 
"He's not disappointed for himself. 
He's disappointed for the team."
Wilson left his teammates to speak for him. 
He exited after the competition without answering questions. 
In his absence, Coach Peter Kormann took the blame for the team's inability to push for a medal.
"The guys did everything I asked them to do," Kormann said. 
"Obviously, my coaching just wasn't good enough. 
It was the coaching; they didn't screw up."
The team's lone triumph was on the parallel bars, where everyone posted scores of 9.7 or better, but it was too late to make up for the bobbles on the floor exercise and the mistakes on the vault. 
In the end, the catastrophes on the horizontal bar didn't doom them. 
The flurry of deductions along the way did.
This wasn't the way Kormann wanted to go out as coach of the team. 
Kormann said he is set to retire Oct. 
1, and does not know who his successor will be. 
If he could recommend someone, it would be the 30-year-old Roethlisberger, who gathered the group for an emotional team meeting after the competition.
"I felt like we were going to win a medal, to be honest," Roethlisberger said, his voice trembling with emotion. 
"I hope America is proud of us. 
We wanted to win for our country, for ourselves, for our family and friends."
In four years, the United States team will try again. 
For 40 years, that has been the mantra in China. 
Next time, next time.
"It's about time," said Peter Vidmar, an NBC analyst and former member of America's 1984 gold medal team. 
"I decided to give China one more chance. 
I said on TV, I'm going to pick them for the gold one more time and never again. 
For the amount of work they've put in, they've been deserving of the gold a long time."
And as the Chinese stood on the podium, the gold medals felt good in their hands.
"We've never touched the gold medal before," said Yang Wei, who led the team by posting no score lower than 9.575. 
"We've only seen it."
Tonight, they had ownership, at last.

file: SYDNEY 2000_ GYMNASTICS_Young Americans Need Focus and Luck.txt
text:
ï»¿
The night Kerri Strug turned a bad ankle into a very good final vault at the 1996 Summer Olympics, Kristen Maloney was already asleep.
"I had a really obnoxious early-morning workout, and it was getting too late, so my mom told me I had to go to bed," Maloney said. 
"But I watched the tape of it the next day, and not just once."
Four years later, Strug has retired and Maloney is the one in the Olympics. 
Like most members of this American women's gymnastics team, she has a difficult act to follow and precious little chance of succeeding.
The 1996 team, which nicknamed itself the Magnificent Seven, became the first American women's gymnastics team to win the gold medal, and it had great depth, ample experience and a significant home-arena advantage. 
Two members of that team have returned -- Dominique Dawes and Amy Chow -- but the rest either failed to qualify (Shannon Miller), suffered injuries (Dominique Moceanu and Jaycie Phelps) or retired (Amanda Borden and Strug).
In their place is a new group of gymnasts, led by Elise Ray, the new national champion. 
But Ray and her teammates could finish only sixth in last year's world championships in China, behind traditional gymnastics powers like Russia, Romania and Ukraine and more troubling, behind the Chinese and weaker Australians.
Closing the gap on Russia and Romania, who finished second and third behind the United States in 1996, is almost certainly too much to ask. 
The Russians are led by Svetlana Khorkina, the reigning European all-around champion whose height, innovative moves and relatively advanced age (21) set her apart from her peers. 
The Russians also have two other gymnasts capable of winning all-around medals: Yelena Zamolodchikova and Yelena Produnova. 
The Romanians are led by Simona Amanar, a bronze medalist in the all-around and gold medalist in the vault at the last Olympic games, and the reigning world champion Maria Olaru.
"It's going to be a fistfight out there," Bela Karolyi, the United States team coordinator, said of the Russian and Romanian duel for the gold medal. 
"It's probably going to be one of the most disputed Olympic Games in history. 
The Russians have been improving for the past 20 years. 
But in Romania, it's still based on an incredible amount of repetitions. 
They have very nicely dedicated athletes."
Ukraine has produced the last two Olympic all-around gold medalists (Tatyana Gutsu in 1992 and Lilya Podkopayeva in 1996) and has another candidate this year in Victoria Karpenko. 
But Ukraine and China appear to lack the depth to challenge for anything but bronze. 
So a medal for the United States team would come as a surprise to the international gymnastics community.
"After the incredible victory in 1996, we probably celebrated a little longer than we should have and had less prominent results in the years after," Karolyi said. 
"But I believe coming down to sixth in the world was a temporary situation. 
I believe the federation handled the matter very well after the world championship. 
It reviewed the power and the unity of the team, and that definitely showed in our national championships and even more through the Olympic trial held in Boston in August. 
The team is strong and united."
The federation's most dramatic move was to lure Karolyi out of retirement and put him in charge. 
But in truth, the team did not look as strong as Karolyi would have liked in Boston, with gymnasts struggling with nerves and routines, particularly on the balance beam. 
Morgan White, one of the team's most consistent performers, was named to the Olympic squad but then had to withdraw because of a stress fracture in her foot. 
She was replaced by Tasha Schwikert, the second alternate. 
Schwikert is 15 but is eligible for the Games because she will turn 16 before the end of the Olympic year.
But Jamie Dantzscher, another member of the team, sprained her ankle in practice on Thursday. 
She is still expected to be in the competition, which begins on Sunday with qualifying. 
Nonetheless, Dantzscher's mishap was one more unsettling incident for a team that will need to be at its most settled and focused. 
Karolyi was also concerned that the team drawing a place in the first of the three qualifying groups would make the task even more difficult.
"You're so cold when you go out before the judges, and you get the cold judgment from the judges," said Karolyi, who as an administrator rather than a coach will not be allowed on the competition floor for the first time in his Olympic career.
The men's team competition, in which China is a heavy favorite to win its first gold, begins on Saturday.

file: The World_Tension With Japan Rises Alongside China_s Star.txt
text:
ï»¿
WHEN the world's athletes converge on Atlanta for the Olympics this summer, there will be one person who Chinese fans fervently hope will lose, will humiliate herself, maybe even have a heart attack during play. 
She is Chire Koyama, Japan's table tennis champion, a strong contender for the gold medal. 
Her sin is that she was born Chinese but then moved to Japan, married a Japanese and joined the Japanese national team.
"Chinese all hate her," explained a Chinese woman living in Japan. 
"After, all, she married a Japanese."
The Chinese fury with Mrs. Koyama is not diminished by the fact that she has an excuse for going to Japan. 
She claims that when she served on the Chinese national team, her coach ordered her to lose a game in the 1987 world championships so that a teammate could advance to the finals. 
Instead, she beat the teammate, and her Chinese coaches reportedly punished her by refusing to allow her to compete in the 1988 Olympics. 
Still, when she began playing for Japan and defeating Chinese players, China's official newspapers denounced her as having been selfish in refusing to throw the match, and as having betrayed her motherland.
The venom underscores the antagonisms that bedevil the delicate relationship between China and Japan, neighbors with histories that have been intertwined for 2,000 years. 
These are the giants of East Asia, two points of a strategic triangle with America, and their relationship is central to continued stabilityII in what is economically the most dynamic part of the world. 
Yet their shared past is more a source of division than of unity, and today distrust is growing rather than receding.
The distrust grew a bit more this month, after China ignored repeated Japanese warnings and conducted a nuclear test underneath its Western desert. 
Because of its memories of the atomic bombs at Hiroshima and Nagasaki, Japan is bitterly hostile to nuclear weapons, and so, perhaps too self-consciously, it interpreted the Chinese nuclear test as a direct insult.
"We are very disappointed," declared Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto as Japan lodged an official protest. 
In Japan's Parliament, there are growing voices for more than just words. 
More and more legislators complain that the Foreign Ministry officials are yowagoshi, roughly meaning spineless, and that politicians must intervene to teach China some respect. 
In particular, some politicians would like to curb Japan's huge loan program to China, while others urge a more aggressive Japanese assertion of ownership over disputed waters and territories. 
The Japanese Government has discouraged Japanese oil companies from exploring for potentially rich deposits of petroleum in waters between the two countries, but some politicians argue that there is no need to be so circumspect.
Â 
Â 
Â 
Hardening Toward Beijing
"There's a growing attitude in Parliament that we need to take a tougher line toward China," said Kazuo Aichi, a former Cabinet member and prominent member of Parliament. 
"Whenever anything happens, the Japanese Government takes too gentle a position, and that's why this impatience is spreading in Parliament."
Yet Mr. Aichi, like almost every senior Japanese official, adds that "the relationship with China will be the major issue for Japan."
It is difficult to have a conversation with a senior Japanese policy maker for more than about 30 minutes before the conversation turns to China, for there is a growing sense that Japan's long-term future is almost as dependent on decisions made in Beijing as in Tokyo. 
"For the last 100 years, our focus in foreign affairs has been on America," said one top official. 
"From now on, it will have to be China."
The concerns in Japan run the gamut: A civil war in China could send tens of millions of boat people fleeing to Japan; a continuing industrial revolution in China could raise global oil prices significantly and send acid rain and other pollutants across the sea to Japan; Chinese adventures against Taiwan or in the South China Sea could interfere with Japan's oil lifeline and cripple economies throughout Asia; an increasingly nationalistic China could seize Japanese islands and confront Japan militarily. 
In America, half a world away, China's rise seems awesome and exciting; in Japan, next door, it also seems awesome but a bit ominous as well.
Â 
Â 
Â 
Suspicion Is Mutual
China, on the other hand, is equally suspicious of Japan. 
Chinese note that whatever its recent problems near its borders, historically China has not been particularly aggressive to its neighbors, while in this century Japan tried to colonize everyone in sight. 
Chinese officials often argue that America is being naive about Japanese militarism, and that Beijing and Washington should team up to contain Japan before it is too late. 
Chinese suspicions are reinforced because Japan always seems half-hearted about apologizing for the deaths of up to 20 million Chinese during World War II.
To be sure, for all the mistrust, Japanese companies have been thrilled by, and shrewd in exploiting, the Chinese market -- somewhat to the chagrin of the Americans, who would prefer allied solidarity in forcing China to respect trade accords. 
Japanese salesmen tend to serve longer tours in China than American counterparts, tend to speak better Chinese, tend to devote more efforts in smaller provincial cities, and, Americans sometimes complain, tend to sweeten deals by making generous "gifts" to Chinese officials. 
But even this interaction stirs Chinese resentment. 
Many Chinese say they would prefer to buy American products, and in 1986 Chinese university students demonstrated against what they called Japan's "economic imperialism."
Such tension belies the ways each side has enriched the other historically. 
Japan was the biggest beneficiary; it learned rice farming from China and much of its language consists of Chinese words. 
It is impossible for a Japanese to converse without using Chinese words, and Japanese culture benefited hugely from Chinese poetry and philosophy. 
"It is because of the Chinese that we are human beings," acknowledged a Japanese official. 
"From them we got writing and even civilization."
The Chinese are also indebted to Japan, for Chinese intellectuals traveled to Japan late in the 19th century and early in this century to study the ideas of the modern world. 
Indeed, most of the Chinese political vocabulary was imported from Japan, including the Chinese words for democracy, politics, economics, government.
These days, some Japanese can be patronizing, even contemptuous, of modern Chinese society. 
But they do not hate Chinese. 
In China, however, local people sometimes tell foreigners that the Chinese character "hen," or hatred, can be defined by "the feeling we Chinese have for the Japanese."
Many Chinese are willing to let their children marry Americans, but a marriage with a Japanese can be a neighborhood scandal.
Â 
Â 
Â 
Looking to Washington
The alarm about China's long-run intentions may be leading Japan to put a greater premium on its security relationship with the United States, since cooperation with America is politically and economically more feasible for Japan than building a first-class army of its own. 
Former Prime Minister Kiichi Miyazawa says bluntly that without the security partnership with Washington, Japan might fully rearm and acquire nuclear weapons. 
Yet like some other senior Japanese officials, Mr. Miyazawa is anxious that alarm about China could become self-fulfilling, by alienating and angering China into becoming just the disruptive force that some fear. 
"Let's not treat China as an enemy," Mr. Miyazawa said. 
"Let's try to engage China in dialogue."

file: To Bolster Olympic Bid, China Eases Its Surveillance of Reporters.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Chinese authorities appear to have stopped following foreign reporters, as part of an effort to spruce up their image and help their bid to become host of the Olympic Games in the year 2000.
The State Security Ministry and Foreign Ministry jointly issued an internal Government circular this month announcing an end to the following of foreign journalists, Chinese familiar with the document say. 
The circular said the step was necessary to improve Beijing's human rights image and therefore its chances of being awarded the Olympic Games.
Beijing is one of half a dozen cities competing to become host of the 2000 Summer Olympics. 
It is vigorously rebuilding roads and renovating its airport in the hopes of winning the Olympics, while also encouraging the use of English and taking other steps to improve its bid.
Considering how security-conscious the Chinese authorities are, the change suggests that they are extremely concerned with the Olympic bid, which is to be decided this fall. 
Diplomats say that China has generally managed its application well and that Beijing will be one of the stronger contenders to get the Olympics.
Â 
An Unusual Vigor
For several years, Government agents have followed certain foreign journalists with a diligence that rarely surfaces in other endeavors. 
While Government ministries often empty by late afternoon, and take days to answer the simplest questions, three carloads of security agents can miraculously appear at 10 on a rainy Saturday night to pursue a foreign reporter.
Reporters for The New York Times, who have apparently been followed more than reporters from any other news organization, were followed almost every time they left their residence in recent months. 
But that kind of surveillance stopped abruptly about 10 days ago, and other journalists said they too had not been followed recently.
Diplomats from the United States and other countries are followed much less frequently than reporters, perhaps because the authorities are less concerned with their secrets getting out than with the embarrassment of having them splashed across foreign newspapers.
The Foreign Ministry and State Council News Office declined today to confirm or deny that the following of reporters had been suspended.
A Foreign Ministry spokesman, asked for a comment, inquired who had told the reporter about the document. 
When the reporter declined to say, the spokesman added that it was difficult to make a comment without this information.
Â 
Harsh Punishment for Chinese
The Government is still extremely concerned with the flow of information to foreign journalists and diplomats, and it has severely punished Chinese accused of giving documents to foreigners. 
The Chinese in such cases are always punished far more harshly than the foreigner.
Wu Shichen, a mid-ranking editor at the official New China News Agency, was detained in October on charges of giving a Hong Kong reporter an advance copy of an important speech. 
Mr. Wu, who is accused of accepting money in exchange for the speech, was recently sentenced to 15 years in prison for revealing state secrets, a Beijing journalist said.
But that sentence seems unusually long and it cannot be confirmed. 
Officials have declined to comment.
The Hong Kong reporter who allegedly paid Mr. Wu for the document was detained for several days and then expelled from the country.
Bai Weiji, a former Foreign Ministry employee who was arrested in May for allegedly giving documents to The Washington Post, remains in custody but has not yet been tried. 
By some accounts, another Chinese who allegedly gave the documents to Mr. Bai may also be awaiting trial.
Chinese security agents searched the office of The Washington Post in May and confiscated what they said were secret documents -- apparently the ones that Mr. Bai is accused of supplying -- but did not expel or take other action against the newspaper's correspondent, Lena H. Sun.
Â 
Electronic Surveillance Goes On
While the following of foreign journalists may be suspended for now, surveillance will presumably continue in more subtle ways. 
Telephones are tapped, offices and homes are bugged, and Chinese are still asked to spy on their foreign acquaintances.
The problem for the security forces is that China has opened up so much in the last few years that surveillance has become more difficult: some Chinese cheerfully cooperate with State Security and then with equal cheerfulness discuss their cooperation with the foreign reporter. 
Others explain the workings of the telephone bugs to those who are being bugged.
Another problem is that State Security docks the salaries of its agents who allow a reporter to get away. 
For fear of losing wages, the agents therefore sometimes disobey orders and stay so close to the reporter that the following is very obvious.

It was 1987, and Cai Weiyan was performing acrobatics at a Chinese sports school.
"A coach who was doing well with men in the pole vault asked me if I liked track and field and did I like pole-vaulting," she recalled yesterday. 
"I was 14. 
I didn't know anything about it. 
He said: 'Are you afraid?
Try it.'
I did. 
The first day, I couldn't clear the bar. 
By the end of the year, I did 3.15 meters" -- 10 feet 4 inches -- "and it was exciting."
In 1989, at another Chinese sports school, Sun Caiyun was playing many sports, including basketball.
"Before that," she said through the same translator, Zhou Xinmin, the manager of the Chinese track team now in New York, "I had no idea about the pole vault. 
A pole-vault coach saw I had a tall body. 
He asked me to try the pole vault. 
I tried it and liked it, but I lacked strength. 
The first time I cleared the bar, I did 2.80 meters," or 9-2 1/4.
Tomorrow night, in the 92d annual Chase Millrose Games at Madison Square Garden, Cai and Sun will compete in the women's pole vault. 
Last year, when America's leading indoor track meet introduced the event, it became one of the competitive highlights of the night. 
This year, with Cai, Sun and Daniela Bartova of the Czech Republic, there is great potential again.
In the 1998 world ranking by Track and Field News, Cai is third and Sun is eighth. 
They are the pioneers of a relatively new sport, which met wide resistance when it was introduced in the United States. 
Too unladylike, critics said.
"It was the same in China," Cai said. 
"When I start to vault, some teammates said this is a dangerous sport. 
I wasn't afraid."
Sun found the same reaction.
"Some friends said it wasn't an Olympic event," she said. 
"Some friends said this is a men's sport not fit for women. 
Now they think I made the right choice."
Good thinking. 
Sun became the first official world record-holder at 13-3 3/4, and five weeks later Cai raised the record to 13-4 1/4. 
In all, Sun has set world records 11 times indoors and 6 times outdoors. 
Their career bests are 14-3 1/4 for Cai and 14- 1/2 for Sun.
The world records are now held by Emma George of Australia -- 15- 3/4 outdoors and 14-11 indoors. 
The progress is amazing in an event for which world records were first recognized only five years ago and which has not yet been contested in a world outdoor championships or Olympics.
Women's pole-vaulting is still an esoteric sport. 
Cai said that perhaps 100 women in all of China are pole-vaulters. 
But last year alone, 17 women from 9 nations cleared 14 feet outdoors, led by George (15- 3/4), Bartova (14-9 1/2) and Stacy Dragila (14-8 1/4), the American record-holder and last year's Millrose winner. 
Dragila is injured now. 
Sun said that if men can clear 6 meters (19-8 1/4), which eight men have done in the last decade, then women can clear 5 meters (16-4 3/4).
But as the bar gets higher, the expectations do, too.
"It used to be a little easier," Cai said, "because China started the event. 
But now it's everywhere and it's high pressure, but it's also an encouragement for the sport."
Cai and Sun are the first Millrose athletes to come from mainland China. 
Li Tong ran in the men's hurdles at Millrose in the 1980's, but at the time he was a student at Washington State, where his name was Americanized to Tony Lee.
The Chinese pole-vaulters are a little Americanized, too. 
When Sun was asked if she knew she would be competing on the same floor where Michael Jordan had performed wonders, her eyes lighted, then saddened. 
"It's a pity,' she said, "that he is retiring from basketball."
